items.title: Founding & the Four Dynasties of Vijayanagara
items.body:
## Foundation (1336 CE)

- **Vijayanagara** ('city of victory') was founded in **1336 CE** by **Harihara I and Bukka Raya I** of the **Sangama** family, with the guidance of **Saint Vidyaranya**.
- Tradition credits five brothers — Harihara, Bukka, Kampana, Mudappa and Marappa — named **Sangamas** after their father.
- The state absorbed the **Hoysala** kingdom by 1346 and was also called the **Karnataka kingdom**.
- Capital: **Hampi** on the **Tungabhadra**, named after goddess **Pampadevi**; the empire stretched from the **river Krishna to the far south**.

## The Four Dynasties

| Dynasty | Period | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Sangama | 1336–1485 | Founders; Deva Raya II a strong king |
| Saluva | 1485–1505 | Brief; Saluva Narasimha |
| Tuluva | 1505–1570 | **Zenith under Krishnadevaraya** |
| Aravidu | 1570–1646 | Last line; decline after Talikota |
keyPoints: Vijayanagara founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I (Sangama dynasty) under Saint Vidyaranya.
The four dynasties in order: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
Capital Hampi on the Tungabhadra, named after goddess Pampadevi; also called the Karnataka kingdom.
The empire stretched from the river Krishna to the far south of the peninsula.
The Hoysala kingdom was absorbed into Vijayanagara by 1346.
items.mnemonic: Dynasty order 'SSTA' = Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu.

items.title: Krishnadevaraya & the Golden Age of Telugu Literature
items.body:
## The Greatest Vijayanagara Ruler

- **Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529)** of the **Tuluva dynasty** took the empire to its **zenith** in territory, culture and prosperity.
- **Babur**, in the **Baburnama**, called him the **most powerful ruler of India**; he is titled **Andhra Bhoja**.
- He kept **cordial relations with the Portuguese**; the traveller **Domingo Paes** visited his court.

## Literary Patronage (AP relevance)

- His court hosted the **Ashtadiggajas** — the **eight greatest poets of Telugu literature** — led by **Allasani Peddana** (titled *Andhra Kavita Pitamaha*); making his reign the **'classic era' of Telugu literature**. His prime minister was **Timmarusu** and the court jester-poet **Tenali Ramakrishna**.
- He built a large **dam across the Tungabhadra** with a canal-cum-aqueduct to Vijayanagara, and won the **Raichur Doab (1520)** and Odisha Gajapati campaigns.
- He was himself an author: **Amuktamalyada** (Telugu, on polity), **Jambavati Kalyanam** (Sanskrit), and **Ushaparinayam** & **Madalasacharita**.
- Other Vijayanagara works: **Gangadevi's Madhuravijayam**; **Vidyaranya's Raja Kalanirnaya**.
keyPoints: Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529, Tuluva) took the empire to its zenith; titled Andhra Bhoja.
Babur's Baburnama called him the most powerful ruler of India.
His court's Ashtadiggajas were the eight greatest Telugu poets — the classic era of Telugu literature.
Allasani Peddana (Andhra Kavita Pitamaha) led the Ashtadiggajas; Timmarusu was PM and Tenali Ramakrishna the court poet.
He built a dam and canal-aqueduct across the Tungabhadra and won the Raichur Doab (1520).
He authored Amuktamalyada (Telugu, polity) and Jambavati Kalyanam (Sanskrit).
He had cordial ties with the Portuguese; Domingo Paes visited his court.
items.mnemonic: 'Andhra Bhoja' = Krishnadevaraya, patron of the eight Telugu 'diggajas'.

items.title: Vijayanagara Administration, Art & Foreign Accounts
items.body:
## Administration

- A **centralised monarchy**: the king held supreme authority, aided by a **council of ministers**.
- Territorial hierarchy (largest → smallest): **Mandala → Nadu → Sthala → Grama**.
- Provinces rested on the **nayankara** system (military chiefs, *nayakas*, holding land grants for troops) and village functionaries (**ayagars**).

## Art & Architecture

- Distinctive **Dravidian** temple style: the **Virupaksha** and **Vittala** temples at Hampi — the latter famous for **musical pillars** and a **stone chariot**.
- Cultural forms: **Carnatic music**, **Kuchipudi** dance, and **Yakshaganam** theatre.

## Foreign Travellers

| Traveller | Identity |
|---|---|
| Nicolo de Conti | Italian explorer |
| Abdur Razzaq | Persian ambassador |
| Domingo Paes | Portuguese traveller |
| Fernao Nunes | Portuguese historian |
keyPoints: Administrative hierarchy: Mandala > Nadu > Sthala > Grama.
The nayankara system granted land to military chiefs (nayakas); ayagars were village functionaries.
Hampi's Vittala temple is famous for musical pillars and a stone chariot (Dravidian style).
Carnatic music, Kuchipudi and Yakshaganam flourished under Vijayanagara.
Key foreign visitors: Nicolo de Conti (Italian), Abdur Razzaq (Persian), Domingo Paes & Fernao Nunes (Portuguese).

items.title: Battle of Talikota (1565) & the Decline
items.body:
## The Turning Point

- The **Battle of Talikota (January 1565)** was fought between **Vijayanagara** (led by **Aliya Rama Raya** of the Aravidu line) and a **coalition of Deccan Sultanates** — **Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar and Bidar**.
- The coalition, led by **Sultan Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur**, won through superior numbers and strategy.
- **Hampi was looted and abandoned**, and the empire fragmented, giving rise to regional powers.

## Why the Long Rivalry?

- The **Raichur doab** (between the **Krishna and Tungabhadra**) was the fertile bone of contention.
- Both states competed over **war-horse imports** (Arabian/Persian, later via the **Portuguese**) and **trade routes**.
- **Religious and territorial** tensions with the Deccan Sultanates sharpened after Vijayanagara grew powerful under Krishnadevaraya.
keyPoints: Battle of Talikota (1565): Vijayanagara under Aliya Rama Raya was crushed by a Deccan Sultanate coalition.
The coalition — Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar — was led by Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur.
Hampi was looted and abandoned; the empire fragmented afterwards.
The Raichur doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra was the core contested region.
War-horse trade (via the Portuguese) and trade routes fuelled the Vijayanagara–Bahmani rivalry.

items.title: Bahmani Kingdom — Founding, Rulers & Mahmud Gawan
items.body:
## Founding (1347 CE)

- Founded by **Alauddin Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)**, an Afghan adventurer, by revolting from the **Delhi Sultanate**.
- First capital **Gulbarga**, later shifted to **Bidar** by **Ahmad Shah Wali (1422–36)**, titled 'Wali' for his link to Sufi saint **Gesu Daraz**.

## Notable Rulers

- **Firoz Shah Bahmani (1397–1422)** — polyglot (Persian, Arabic, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi), built a **Daulatabad observatory**, and inducted **Hindus** into administration.
- **Muhammad Shah III (1463–82)** — ascended at nine, with **Mahmud Gawan** as regent.

## Mahmud Gawan

- An **Iranian trader** who became **Prime Minister**; conquered Goa, Dabhol, Konkan, Orissa and campaigned against Vijayanagara.
- Introduced **revenue reforms** and built the famous **three-storeyed madrasa at Bidar** (housing 1,000 students).
- **Executed in 1482** through nobles' conspiracies — hastening the kingdom's decline.
keyPoints: Bahmani Kingdom founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu), an Afghan adventurer.
Capital shifted Gulbarga → Bidar by Ahmad Shah Wali (linked to Sufi saint Gesu Daraz).
Firoz Shah Bahmani was a polyglot who built a Daulatabad observatory and included Hindus in administration.
Mahmud Gawan, an Iranian trader, became PM, reformed revenue, and built the Bidar madrasa.
Mahmud Gawan was executed in 1482, accelerating the Bahmani decline.

items.title: Bahmani Administration, Break-up & Deccan Sultanates
items.body:
## Administration

- Divided into **eight provinces (tarafs)**, each under a **Tarafdar** (major ones: Gulbarga, Bidar, Berar, Daulatabad).
- Nobles paid in **cash or jagirs**; the nobility split between **Deccanis** (local Muslims) and **Afaqis/Pardesis** (immigrants from Iran, Iraq, Central Asia) — a chronic source of conflict.
- Army relied on the **Amirs** and used **gunpowder** in warfare.

## Break-up into Five Deccan Sultanates (by 1526)

| Sultanate | Dynasty | Founder |
|---|---|---|
| Bijapur | Adil Shahi | Yusuf Adil Shah |
| Ahmednagar | Nizam Shahi | Malik Ahmad |
| Golconda | Qutub Shahi | Quli Qutub Shah |
| Berar | Imad Shahi | Fatullah Imad Shah |
| Bidar | Barid Shahi | Amir Ali Barid |

## Architecture & Literature

- Persian-style: tall minarets, arches, large domes — **Gol Gumbaz** (Bijapur, largest dome in Asia), **Ibrahim Roza** (Bijapur), **Charminar** (Hyderabad, by Muhammad Quli Qutub Shah).
- **Dakhini Urdu** flourished; **Gesu Daraz** and **Mahmud Gawan** (Riyaz-ul-Insha, Manazir-ul-Insha) were key literary figures.
keyPoints: Bahmani kingdom had eight tarafs under Tarafdars; nobles paid in cash or jagirs.
Nobility split into Deccanis (local) and Afaqis/Pardesis (immigrants) — a chronic rivalry; army used gunpowder.
Broke up (by 1526) into five Deccan Sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmednagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutub Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi).
Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur) has the largest dome in Asia; Charminar was built by Muhammad Quli Qutub Shah at Hyderabad.
Dakhini Urdu flourished; Gesu Daraz and Mahmud Gawan (Riyaz-ul-Insha) were key writers.
items.mnemonic: Five Sultanates 'BAGBB' = Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda, Berar, Bidar.
